issues.legal_issue: An institution and its associated properties are a public trust when their origin, public use, public support, and overall circumstances establish that character.
material_facts: The institution was built on land granted by the ruler, and the ruler also made provision for its upkeep.
Devotees made substantial contributions and gifts of property, including donations for repairs and expansion.
Members of the public had access to worship, religious festivities were held on a grand scale, and collection boxes were placed for devotees’ offerings.
The State had treated the institution as a temple, and the evidence included public involvement in its maintenance and management.
The High Court assessed the evidence as a whole and found the institution and thirty-eight properties to be a public trust; two other properties were no longer in dispute.
issues.conclusion: The Court affirmed that the Haveli and the thirty-eight listed properties constituted a public trust under the Act.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 2(13) and 2(17) of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950, the character of a temple depends on the relevant facts and circumstances. The Court relied on Tilkayat Shri Govindlalji Maharaj v. The State of Rajasthan, which held that Vallabha tenets do not preclude public temples, and Goswami Shri Mahalaxmi Vahuji v. Rannchhoddas Kalidas, which identified circumstances relevant to deciding whether a temple is public, including public access, public contributions, religious observances, and how the institution is treated. The circumstances must be considered together rather than treating any one feature as conclusive.

rule.if: public_trust_status_appeal and (public_worship_and_religious_observances or public_contributions_and_state_support) and total_evidence_supports_public_character

predicates.public_trust_status_appeal: The proceeding asks whether an institution and its associated property have the character of a public trust.
predicates.public_worship_and_religious_observances: Members of the public worship at the institution and religious observances are held there.
predicates.public_contributions_and_state_support: Devotees and public authorities contribute property, money, or other support to the institution.
predicates.total_evidence_supports_public_character: The court assesses the relevant circumstances together and finds that, taken as a whole, they support public character.

issues.definition: When a public-trust-status appeal concerns an institution where public worship or religious observances occur, public contributions or state support are present, and the overall evidence supports public character, the institution and its associated properties are a public trust.

issues.legal_issue: Succession to trusteeship may occur by inheritance without State approval.
material_facts: The High Court found that the appellant was trustee of the temple and its properties and that succession to trusteeship was by inheritance without the sanction of the State Government.
The Supreme Court affirmed that finding.
issues.conclusion: The Court affirmed that succession to trusteeship was by inheritance without the sanction of the State.
issues.legal_principle: The Court affirmed the High Court’s finding on the mode of succession. The judgment cites no separate statutory provision or earlier case as the basis for this conclusion.

predicates.trusteeship_succession_issue: The proceeding concerns how trusteeship of a religious institution passes to a successor.
predicates.succession_to_trusteeship_occurs_by_inhe: The trustee’s successor takes trusteeship through inheritance.

issues.definition: When a proceeding concerns succession to trusteeship and the successor takes through inheritance, trusteeship passes by inheritance without State approval.

issues.legal_issue: Offerings made personally at the feet of a religious preceptor, or to him while travelling, belong to the preceptor rather than the public trust unless evidence shows that they were intended for the deity or trust.
material_facts: Devotees customarily made offerings at the feet of the religious preceptor when meeting him, and made similar offerings when meeting him outside the institution during his travels.
The Court distinguished offerings made before the deity or placed in a collection box from offerings made at the preceptor’s feet.
The record did not establish that the preceptor was merely a conduit for offerings to the deity or that these offerings were intended for the deity.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the proceeds of Guruseva and Pradesh Seva did not constitute part of the public trust.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar of Sri Shirur Mutt, noting that the treatment of personal gifts to a religious head supports treating offerings at the head’s feet as personal. An offering before the deity or into a collection box is an offering to the deity; an offering at the preceptor’s feet is, absent evidence to the contrary, an offering to the preceptor.

rule.if: offering_character_proceeding and offering_made_to_preceptor_personally and not evidence_of_intent_for_deity_or_trust

predicates.offering_character_proceeding: The proceeding concerns whether offerings associated with a religious institution belong to its public trust.
predicates.offering_made_to_preceptor_personally: A devotee gives an offering at the religious preceptor’s feet or directly to him while he is travelling.
predicates.evidence_of_intent_for_deity_or_trust: Evidence shows that the offering was intended for the deity or the public trust.

issues.definition: When a proceeding concerns ownership of offerings made personally to a preceptor, and there is no evidence that they were intended for the deity or trust, the offering belongs to the preceptor rather than the public trust.

issues.legal_issue: A purchaser cannot enforce a claim to property held to belong to a public trust on the basis of an agreement made with the trustee during litigation over the property’s status.
material_facts: The purchasers entered into an agreement with the trustee to buy certain properties while litigation arising from the statutory inquiry was pending.
The properties were held to belong to the public trust.
issues.conclusion: The purchasers had no claim to enforce, and their appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that once the properties were determined to belong to the public trust, the purchasers could not enforce their agreement-based claim against them. The judgment cites no separate statutory provision or earlier case for this conclusion.

predicates.purchaser_claim_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal by a purchaser seeking to enforce a claim to property.
predicates.purchase_agreement_made_during_pending_t: The purchaser entered into an agreement with the trustee while litigation concerning the property’s trust status was pending.
predicates.property_belongs_to_public_trust: The property is held to belong to a public trust.

issues.definition: When a purchaser appeals to enforce a claim based on an agreement made during pending litigation over trust status, and the property belongs to a public trust, the purchaser has no enforceable claim to the property.
